m-dbscan-gmm.data: **Palmer penguins** — 344 real penguins measured in Antarctica: species, island, bill length/depth, flipper length, body mass ([palmerpenguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/)).

steps.h: DBSCAN on bill length + bill depth
steps.md:
A penguin with at least 10 neighbours within radius 0.35 (in standardised units) is a core point; connected core points form a cluster; the rest is noise:

| DBSCAN | Adelie | Chinstrap | Gentoo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cluster 0 | 129 | 4 | 0 |
| cluster 1 | 0 | 19 | 111 |
| cluster 2 | 0 | 33 | 0 |
| noise | 17 | 12 | 8 |

Nobody told it there are 3 groups: it found 3.

| eps (radius) | clusters found | noise points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.25 | 3 | 127 |
| 0.35 | 3 | 37 |
| 0.5 | 1 | 9 |

Too small: lots of penguins are thrown away as noise. Too big: everything merges into one blob.

Most penguins belong almost 100% to one group. These four are the least certain:

| species | bill_length_mm | flipper_length_mm | P(group 0) | P(group 1) | P(group 2) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chinstrap | 42.5 | 187 | 0.46 | 0 | 0.54 |
| Chinstrap | 42.5 | 187 | 0.62 | 0 | 0.38 |
| Chinstrap | 46 | 195 | 0.72 | 0 | 0.28 |
| Adelie | 43.1 | 197 | 0.27 | 0 | 0.73 |

k-means would force each of them into one group; the mixture says how unsure it is.
DBSCAN: unknown number of groups, odd shapes, want noise marked. Gaussian mixture: overlapping groups and you want probabilities of belonging.

m-dbscan-gmm.takeaway: DBSCAN follows dense regions and labels outliers; Gaussian mixtures give each point a probability per group.

m-curse-dim.data: **Handwritten digits** — 1,797 real scanned handwritten digits, 8 × 8 pixels each, values 0–16 ([UCI](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/80/optical+recognition+of+handwritten+digits)).

steps.md:
From the first scanned digit to all 1,796 others, using a random subset of pixels:

| pixels used | nearest distance | average distance | farthest distance | nearest as % of average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 0 | 0.34 | 0.76 | 0% |
| 8 | 0.2 | 0.77 | 1.4 | 26% |
| 32 | 0.38 | 1.77 | 2.61 | 21% |
| 64 | 0.68 | 2.87 | 3.96 | 24% |

With only 2 pixels some other image matches exactly (distance 0). With 8–64 pixels the nearest real digit stays at about 21%–26% of the average distance: neighbours are still clearly closer than everything else.

Random points with 1,000 features: nearest 12.0, average 12.8, farthest 13.4; the nearest point is **94%** of the average distance. Everything is almost equally far, so 'nearest neighbour' means almost nothing.
Real images are not random: pixels are strongly related, so the digits actually live on a much lower-dimensional surface. That's why PCA and embeddings work.

m-curse-dim.takeaway: In many dimensions, random points are all about equally far apart; real data escapes this only because it has structure.

m-pca.data: **Palmer penguins** — 344 real penguins measured in Antarctica: species, island, bill length/depth, flipper length, body mass ([palmerpenguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/)).

steps.h: How much each new axis keeps

steps.md:
|  | PC1 | PC2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bill_length_mm | 0.45 | 0.6 |
| bill_depth_mm | -0.4 | 0.8 |
| flipper_length_mm | 0.58 | 0.01 |
| body_mass_g | 0.55 | 0.08 |

PC1 mixes flipper length, body mass and bill length (with bill depth the other way): it's roughly **overall size**. PC2 is mostly bill shape.

steps.h: Real penguins on the new axes
steps.md:
| species | PC1 | PC2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adelie | -1.85 | 0.03 |
| Chinstrap | -0.3 | 1.98 |
| Gentoo | 1.85 | -0.83 |

Species averages on PC1/PC2:

| species | PC1 | PC2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adelie | -1.46 | -0.14 |
| Chinstrap | -0.39 | 0.99 |
| Gentoo | 2.01 | -0.39 |

Gentoos sit far along PC1 (big birds); Adelie and Chinstrap separate on PC2 (bill shape).

m-pca.takeaway: PCA finds new axes ordered by how much the data varies along them; the first few often have a clear meaning.

m-eigenfaces.data: **Handwritten digits** — 1,797 real scanned handwritten digits, 8 × 8 pixels each, values 0–16 ([UCI](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/80/optical+recognition+of+handwritten+digits)).

steps.h: Every digit = mean + a mix of component images
steps.md: Each principal component reshaped to 8 × 8 is an 'eigen-digit' (for faces, an eigenface). A digit is described by how much of each it contains.

| components kept | numbers per image | avg pixel error after rebuild (0-16) | digit accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 2 | 2.514 | 0.64 |
| 5 | 5 | 1.982 | 0.9 |
| 10 | 10 | 1.5 | 0.964 |
| 20 | 20 | 0.989 | 0.984 |
| 40 | 40 | 0.287 | 0.987 |

With all 64 raw pixels the same classifier scores **99.1%**. 20 numbers per image instead of 64 rebuild the digits closely and score 98.4%.

m-eigenfaces.takeaway: Eigenfaces/eigen-digits compress images into a short code of component weights that still identifies them.

m-lda.data: **Wine** — 178 real Italian wines from three cultivars, with 13 chemical measurements ([UCI](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/109/wine)).

steps.md:
Chosen so the cultivars' averages are far apart and each cultivar is tight:

| cultivar | LD1_mean | LD1_spread | LD2_mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C1 | -3.45 | 0.95 | 1.71 |
| C2 | -0.08 | 1.09 | -2.49 |
| C3 | 4.36 | 0.95 | 1.59 |
Reduce to 2 numbers, then classify with nearest neighbours: PCA **96.6%**, LDA **98.9%**.

m-lda.takeaway: LDA uses the labels to find the directions that best separate the classes.

m-manifold.data: **Handwritten digits** — 1,797 real scanned handwritten digits, 8 × 8 pixels each, values 0–16 ([UCI](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/80/optical+recognition+of+handwritten+digits)).

steps.md: Each digit image has 64 pixel values, impossible to look at directly.

A good 2-D map keeps similar digits next to each other. Measure it by asking how often a point's 5 nearest neighbours on the map are the same digit:

| method | neighbours share the same digit |
| --- | --- |
| PCA to 2-D | 0.564 |
| t-SNE to 2-D | 0.946 |
t-SNE gives ten clean islands, one per digit, because it only tries to keep neighbours together. The sizes of the islands and the distances between them don't mean anything.

m-manifold.takeaway: Manifold methods like t-SNE and UMAP keep neighbourhoods, which makes clusters visible in 2-D.

m-anomaly.data: **California housing** — real 1990 US census districts: median income, house age, rooms, population, location and median house value (3,000-district sample of the 20,640; [StatLib via *Hands-On ML*](https://github.com/ageron/handson-ml2)). **Titanic passengers** — 891 real passengers of the 1912 sinking, with class, sex, age, fare and whether they survived ([Kaggle / Data Science Dojo](https://github.com/datasciencedojo/datasets)).

steps.md:
Most districts have 4–7 rooms per household. The most extreme:

| rooms_per_household | population | households | ocean_proximity | z |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 50.8 | 64 | 37 | INLAND | 20.5 |
| 41.3 | 44 | 21 | INLAND | 16.2 |
| 38.8 | 97 | 44 | INLAND | 15.1 |
| 36.5 | 291 | 115 | INLAND | 14 |

A z-score above 3 means 'more than 3 standard deviations from the average'. Tiny populations with huge numbers of rooms per household: most likely holiday-home areas, or a data quirk worth checking. Either way, a human should look.
Fares above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = £66 count as outliers: 116 passengers, 90% of them first class. Outliers aren't errors; they are rare cases to look at.

m-anomaly.takeaway: Anomaly detection learns what normal looks like and flags what doesn't fit; a human decides if it's an error, fraud or just rare.

m-recsys.data: **Goodreads ratings** — real 1–5 star ratings from 600 Goodreads readers of the 40 most-rated books ([goodbooks-10k](https://github.com/zygmuntz/goodbooks-10k)).

steps.h: Real ratings: most cells are empty
steps.md:
17,857 ratings from 600 readers on 40 books; **26%** of the reader × book table is blank. Reader 196 rated 28 books, e.g.:

| title | stars |
| --- | --- |
| Gone Girl | 5 |
| Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire | 5 |
| Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows | 5 |
| Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets | 5 |
| Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoeni | 5 |

Correlate reader 196's ratings with every other reader on the books both rated (at least 8 in common):

| user_id | similarity |

| 30,307 | 0.83 |
| 4,444 | 0.82 |
| 8,652 | 0.8 |

Highest predicted ratings among books they haven't rated:

m-assoc-rules.data: **Restaurant tips** — 244 real restaurant bills recorded by a waiter: total bill, tip, day, time, party size.

steps.h: Each bill as a 'basket' of properties
steps.md: 244 real restaurant bills, turned into yes/no properties such as Sunday, Dinner, Smoker, Party of 4+, Big tip, Big bill.

| if | then | support | confidence | lift |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Smoker | Party of 4+ | 0.05 | 0.14 | 0.74 |
| Sunday | Smoker | 0.08 | 0.25 | 0.66 |
| Smoker | Sunday | 0.08 | 0.2 | 0.66 |

Lift above 1: the 'if' part makes the 'then' part more likely; below 1, less likely.

m-assoc-rules.takeaway: Association rules turn co-occurrence counts into 'if A then B' rules, ranked by support, confidence and lift.

m-linear-classification.data: **Palmer penguins** — 344 real penguins measured in Antarctica: species, island, bill length/depth, flipper length, body mass ([palmerpenguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/)).

steps.md:
265 real Adelie and Gentoo penguins, 2 measurements each. Every method learns a score w·x + b and draws the line where it is 0:

| method | boundary (real units) | training accuracy | closest penguin to the line (sd units) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| perceptron | flipper = 67.7 + 8.52 × bill depth | 1 | 0.173 |
| logistic regression | flipper = 101.3 + 6.29 × bill depth | 1 | 0.228 |
| linear SVM | flipper = 99.9 + 6.42 × bill depth | 1 | 0.278 |
| LDA | flipper = 117.2 + 5.20 × bill depth | 1 | 0.042 |

All four separate the species perfectly, but they pick different lines. The **linear SVM** leaves the widest gap to the nearest penguin, because maximising that gap (the margin) is exactly what it optimises.

Logistic regression's score for three penguins (positive → Gentoo):

| species | bill_depth_mm | flipper_length_mm | score w·x + b | prediction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adelie | 18 | 210 | -0.89 | Adelie |
| Adelie | 18.7 | 181 | -7.56 | Adelie |
| Gentoo | 16.1 | 213 | 2.09 | Gentoo |

The first one is the penguin nearest the line: its score is close to 0, so it's the least certain.

steps.h: When a straight line isn't enough
steps.md: Adelie vs Chinstrap on the same two measurements: their clouds overlap, and the best line is right only **74%** of the time (5-fold). Switching to bill length + bill depth, where Chinstraps stand out, the same linear model scores **97%**: often the fix is a better feature, not a more complex model.

m-linear-classification.takeaway: Linear classifiers all predict by which side of a straight line a point falls on; the method only decides which line, and good features decide whether a line can work at all.

m-naive-bayes.data: **SMS Spam Collection** — 5,572 real text messages from the UK and Singapore, each labelled spam or ham (normal) ([UCI](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/228/sms+spam+collection)).

steps.h: Score a new message by hand
steps.md: “free call now”: spam score = log P(spam) + Σ log P(word ∣ spam) = **-16.00**; ham score = **-18.52**. P(spam) = 1 / (1 + e^(ham − spam)) = **0.9256**; scikit-learn gives 0.9256. Words multiply their evidence, so three mildly spam-ish words together make spam very likely.

Test spam F1 on 1,393 unseen messages (averaged over 5 random training sets for the small sizes):

| labelled messages | Naive Bayes spam F1 | logistic regression spam F1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 | 0.457 | 0.096 |
| 100 | 0.744 | 0.386 |
| 4,179 | 0.927 | 0.927 |

With few labels Naive Bayes beats logistic regression clearly; with all the data they end up close.

m-naive-bayes.takeaway: Naive Bayes multiplies per-word evidence with the class prior; it's crude but fast and especially strong when labelled data is scarce.

m-discriminant-analysis.data: **Palmer penguins** — 344 real penguins measured in Antarctica: species, island, bill length/depth, flipper length, body mass ([palmerpenguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/)).

steps.md: Flipper length of 265 real penguins. Adelie mean **190.1 mm**, Gentoo mean **217.2 mm**, pooled spread (sd) **6.6 mm**; 55% of them are Adelie. LDA's boundary = midpoint 203.7 + sd² × ln(P(Gentoo)/P(Adelie)) / (mean_A − mean_G) = 203.7 +0.32 = **204.0 mm**. The more common species gets a little extra room. This single cut classifies 98.5% of the penguins correctly.

| model | 5-fold accuracy |
| --- | --- |
| LDA (shared spread, straight boundaries) | 0.982 |
| QDA (own spread per class, curved) | 0.985 |
| logistic regression | 0.985 |

With 333 penguins all three do about equally well: the species really are roughly Gaussian clouds.

steps.h: Why LDA is the safer choice with little data
steps.md: Train on only **6 penguins per species**, test on the rest (10 repeats): LDA **97.4%**, QDA **86.2%**. QDA must estimate a separate 4 × 4 spread matrix for each species from 6 birds; LDA pools all 18 into one.

m-discriminant-analysis.takeaway: LDA and QDA classify by asking which class's Gaussian cloud a point most likely came from; shared spread gives straight, stable boundaries, separate spreads give curved ones that need more data.

m-threshold-calibration.data: **Breast cancer (Wisconsin)** — 569 real biopsies: 30 measurements of cell nuclei and whether the tumour was malignant or benign ([UCI](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast+cancer+wisconsin+diagnostic)).

steps.md:
Logistic regression on 228 unseen real biopsies (85 malignant):

| threshold | malignant caught (recall) | flagged that are malignant (precision) | cancers missed | benign flagged |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.05 | 0.98 | 0.75 | 2 | 27 |
| 0.2 | 0.95 | 0.86 | 4 | 13 |
| 0.5 | 0.92 | 0.97 | 7 | 2 |
| 0.8 | 0.88 | 1 | 10 | 0 |
| 0.95 | 0.82 | 1 | 15 | 0 |

A hospital would accept a few extra benign biopsies flagged to miss as few cancers as possible, so it picks a low threshold, not 0.5.

Naive Bayes is very sure of itself: 91% of its predictions are below 0.001 or above 0.999. Grouping predictions and comparing with what really happened:

| predicted P(malignant) | raw naive Bayes | calibrated naive Bayes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| below 0.1 | 140 biopsies, said 0.00, really 0.06 | 124 biopsies, said 0.01, really 0.02 |
| 0.1–0.9 | 4 biopsies, said 0.31, really 0.25 | 29 biopsies, said 0.59, really 0.34 |
| above 0.9 | 84 biopsies, said 1.00, really 0.90 | 75 biopsies, said 0.97, really 0.97 |

Brier score (lower = better): raw **0.073**, after isotonic calibration **0.060**.

If missing a cancer is judged 20× worse than an unnecessary follow-up, flag when P(malignant) > 1/(1 + 20) = **0.048**. With logistic regression's probabilities that flags 110 of 228 biopsies and misses 2 cancers. This only works if the probabilities are calibrated, which is why the two steps go together.

m-threshold-calibration.takeaway: Choose the threshold from the cost of each mistake, and make sure the probabilities it's applied to are calibrated.

m-choosing-classifier.data: **Titanic passengers** — 891 real passengers of the 1912 sinking, with class, sex, age, fare and whether they survived ([Kaggle / Data Science Dojo](https://github.com/datasciencedojo/datasets)).

steps.h: Same data, same folds, same metric
steps.md: 891 real passengers, 7 columns (missing ages filled and categories encoded inside each model's pipeline, so no test fold leaks into training). Every model is scored on the **same** 10 folds (5-fold, repeated twice) by AUC.

| model | AUC mean | ± sd across folds | time (s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gradient boosting | 0.869 | 0.028 | 0.61 |
| random forest | 0.868 | 0.031 | 3.44 |
| kNN (k = 15) | 0.851 | 0.032 | 0.19 |
| LDA | 0.849 | 0.037 | 0.18 |
| logistic regression | 0.849 | 0.035 | 0.19 |
| SVM (RBF kernel) | 0.845 | 0.041 | 0.24 |
| decision tree (depth 4) | 0.843 | 0.032 | 0.18 |
| naive Bayes | 0.83 | 0.032 | 0.17 |
| always 'died' (baseline) | 0.5 | 0 | 0.17 |

Compare fold by fold with logistic regression: **gradient boosting** is ahead by +0.020 AUC, about 3.5 standard errors, so the gain is probably real. Models statistically tied with logistic regression here: LDA, kNN (k = 15), decision tree (depth 4), SVM (RBF kernel). Final pick depends on the job: the top model for pure accuracy, logistic regression if every decision must be explained, with the gap above as the price of explainability.

m-choosing-classifier.takeaway: Choose a classifier by comparing several families on identical folds with the right metric, then weigh any real gain against simplicity and explainability.
